claim: UBE3A encodes ubiquitin protein ligase E3A.
source: UBE3A encodes ubiquitin protein ligase E3A, and in neurons its expression from the paternal allele is repressed by the UBE3A antisense transcript (UBE3A-ATS).
evidence: This is a well-established fact stated in the abstract and supported by the scientific literature on Angelman syndrome.

claim: In neurons, UBE3A expression from the paternal allele is repressed by the UBE3A antisense transcript (UBE3A-ATS).
source: UBE3A encodes ubiquitin protein ligase E3A, and in neurons its expression from the paternal allele is repressed by the UBE3A antisense transcript (UBE3A-ATS).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is a fundamental mechanism of UBE3A imprinting.

claim: Angelman syndrome is caused by maternal UBE3A deficiency.
source: Indeed, Angelman syndrome, a severe neurodevelopmental disorder, is caused by maternal UBE3A deficiency.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field and is stated explicitly in the abstract.

claim: A promising therapeutic approach to treating Angelman syndrome is to reactivate the intact paternal UBE3A by suppressing UBE3A-ATS.
source: A promising therapeutic approach to treating Angelman syndrome is to reactivate the intact paternal UBE3A by suppressing UBE3A-ATS.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a therapeutic strategy and is supported by the study's experimental design.

claim: Many neurological phenotypes of maternal Ube3a knockout mice can only be rescued by reinstating Ube3a expression in early development.
source: Prior studies show that many neurological phenotypes of maternal Ube3a knockout mice can only be rescued by reinstating Ube3a expression in early development, indicating a restricted therapeutic window for Angelman syndrome.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies and is stated explicitly in the abstract.

claim: The therapeutic window for Angelman syndrome is restricted to early development.
source: Prior studies show that many neurological phenotypes of maternal Ube3a knockout mice can only be rescued by reinstating Ube3a expression in early development, indicating a restricted therapeutic window for Angelman syndrome.
evidence: This is an inference from prior studies cited in the abstract.

claim: Reducing Ube3a-ATS by antisense oligonucleotides in juvenile or adult maternal Ube3a knockout mice rescues abnormal EEG rhythms.
source: Here, we report that reducing Ube3a-ATS by antisense oligonucleotides in juvenile or adult maternal Ube3a knockout mice rescues the abnormal electroencephalogram (EEG) rhythms and sleep disturbance, two prominent clinical features of Angelman syndrome.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Reducing Ube3a-ATS by antisense oligonucleotides in juvenile or adult maternal Ube3a knockout mice rescues sleep disturbance.
source: Here, we report that reducing Ube3a-ATS by antisense oligonucleotides in juvenile or adult maternal Ube3a knockout mice rescues the abnormal electroencephalogram (EEG) rhythms and sleep disturbance, two prominent clinical features of Angelman syndrome.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Abnormal EEG rhythms and sleep disturbance are two prominent clinical features of Angelman syndrome.
source: Here, we report that reducing Ube3a-ATS by antisense oligonucleotides in juvenile or adult maternal Ube3a knockout mice rescues the abnormal electroencephalogram (EEG) rhythms and sleep disturbance, two prominent clinical features of Angelman syndrome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by clinical knowledge of Angelman syndrome.

claim: The degree of phenotypic improvement correlates with the increase of Ube3a protein levels.
source: Importantly, the degree of phenotypic improvement correlates with the increase of Ube3a protein levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by correlation analyses in Figure 8.

claim: The therapeutic window of genetic therapies for Angelman syndrome is broader than previously thought.
source: These results indicate that the therapeutic window of genetic therapies for Angelman syndrome is broader than previously thought, and EEG power spectrum and sleep architecture should be used to evaluate the clinical efficacy of therapies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings that ASO treatment is effective in juvenile and adult mice.

claim: EEG power spectrum and sleep architecture should be used to evaluate the clinical efficacy of therapies for Angelman syndrome.
source: These results indicate that the therapeutic window of genetic therapies for Angelman syndrome is broader than previously thought, and EEG power spectrum and sleep architecture should be used to evaluate the clinical efficacy of therapies.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings that these measures are responsive to ASO treatment.

claim: Angelman syndrome is characterized by severe intellectual disability, developmental delay, speech impairment, motor dysfunction, behavioral uniqueness, microcephaly, sleep disturbance, seizures, and abnormal electroencephalogram (EEG).
source: Angelman syndrome is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by severe intellectual disability, developmental delay, speech impairment, motor dysfunction, behavioral uniqueness, microcephaly, sleep disturbance, seizures, and abnormal electroencephalogram (EEG) (Williams et al., 2006; Bird, 2014; Buiting et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Angelman syndrome is caused by loss-of-function of the maternally derived UBE3A gene.
source: It is caused by loss-of-function of the maternally derived UBE3A gene encoding ubiquitin protein ligase E3A (Kishino et al., 1997; Matsuura et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to foundational studies.

claim: UBE3A is expressed from both maternal and paternal alleles in non-neuronal cells.
source: UBE3A is expressed from both maternal and paternal alleles in non-neuronal cells, but is paternally imprinted in neurons (Albrecht et al., 1997; Rougeulle et al., 1997; Judson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: UBE3A is paternally imprinted in neurons.
source: UBE3A is expressed from both maternal and paternal alleles in non-neuronal cells, but is paternally imprinted in neurons (Albrecht et al., 1997; Rougeulle et al., 1997; Judson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Imprinted expression of UBE3A in neurons is due to UBE3A-ATS.
source: Imprinted expression of UBE3A or silence of the paternal allele in neurons is due to a long non-coding RNA, UBE3A antisense transcript (UBE3A-ATS).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is a well-established mechanism.

claim: UBE3A-ATS is expressed from the paternally inherited chromosome.
source: UBE3A-ATS is expressed from the paternally inherited chromosome and localized in the nucleus to repress UBE3A in cis through a transcriptional collision mechanism (Meng et al., 2012; Meng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: UBE3A-ATS represses UBE3A in cis through a transcriptional collision mechanism.
source: UBE3A-ATS is expressed from the paternally inherited chromosome and localized in the nucleus to repress UBE3A in cis through a transcriptional collision mechanism (Meng et al., 2012; Meng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Loss-of-function of maternal UBE3A leads to the absence of functional UBE3A proteins in neurons.
source: Thus, loss-of-function of the maternal UBE3A leads to the absence of functional UBE3A proteins in neurons.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the imprinting mechanism stated in the introduction.

claim: Deletions in the chromosomal region 15q11–q13 containing UBE3A account for about 70% of Angelman syndrome patients.
source: Maternal UBE3A deficiency can result from deletions in the chromosomal region 15q11–q13 containing UBE3A, which account for about 70% of Angelman syndrome patients, mutations in UBE3A gene, paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15, or an imprinting defect (Williams et al., 2006; Bird, 2014; Buiting et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Maternal Ube3a deficiency in mice causes motor impairments.
source: Many disease relevant phenotypes were reported in these Angelman syndrome models (Margolis et al., 2015; Rotaru et al., 2020; Yang, 2020), and some of them are robust and reproducible in different models and laboratories, including motor impairments (e.g., poor performance in rotarod and open-field tests), decreased innate marble burying and nest building behaviors, cortical hyperexcitability (e.g, poly-spikes in EEG), altered EEG power spectrum and sleep pattern, increased susceptibility to seizure induction, and reduced synaptic long-term potentiation (Jiang et al., 1998; Miura et al., 2002; Weeber et al., 2003; Colas et al., 2005; Yashiro et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2013; Ehlen et al., 2015; Silva-Santos et al., 2015; Judson et al., 2016; Born et al., 2017; Sidorov et al., 2017; Sonzogni et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2019; Copping and Silverman, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Maternal Ube3a deficiency in mice causes decreased innate marble burying and nest building behaviors.
source: Many disease relevant phenotypes were reported in these Angelman syndrome models (Margolis et al., 2015; Rotaru et al., 2020; Yang, 2020), and some of them are robust and reproducible in different models and laboratories, including motor impairments (e.g., poor performance in rotarod and open-field tests), decreased innate marble burying and nest building behaviors, cortical hyperexcitability (e.g, poly-spikes in EEG), altered EEG power spectrum and sleep pattern, increased susceptibility to seizure induction, and reduced synaptic long-term potentiation (Jiang et al., 1998; Miura et al., 2002; Weeber et al., 2003; Colas et al., 2005; Yashiro et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2013; Ehlen et al., 2015; Silva-Santos et al., 2015; Judson et al., 2016; Born et al., 2017; Sidorov et al., 2017; Sonzogni et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2019; Copping and Silverman, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Maternal Ube3a deficiency in mice causes cortical hyperexcitability.
source: Many disease relevant phenotypes were reported in these Angelman syndrome models (Margolis et al., 2015; Rotaru et al., 2020; Yang, 2020), and some of them are robust and reproducible in different models and laboratories, including motor impairments (e.g., poor performance in rotarod and open-field tests), decreased innate marble burying and nest building behaviors, cortical hyperexcitability (e.g, poly-spikes in EEG), altered EEG power spectrum and sleep pattern, increased susceptibility to seizure induction, and reduced synaptic long-term potentiation (Jiang et al., 1998; Miura et al., 2002; Weeber et al., 2003; Colas et al., 2005; Yashiro et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2013; Ehlen et al., 2015; Silva-Santos et al., 2015; Judson et al., 2016; Born et al., 2017; Sidorov et al., 2017; Sonzogni et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2019; Copping and Silverman, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Maternal Ube3a deficiency in mice causes altered EEG power spectrum and sleep pattern.
source: Many disease relevant phenotypes were reported in these Angelman syndrome models (Margolis et al., 2015; Rotaru et al., 2020; Yang, 2020), and some of them are robust and reproducible in different models and laboratories, including motor impairments (e.g., poor performance in rotarod and open-field tests), decreased innate marble burying and nest building behaviors, cortical hyperexcitability (e.g, poly-spikes in EEG), altered EEG power spectrum and sleep pattern, increased susceptibility to seizure induction, and reduced synaptic long-term potentiation (Jiang et al., 1998; Miura et al., 2002; Weeber et al., 2003; Colas et al., 2005; Yashiro et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2013; Ehlen et al., 2015; Silva-Santos et al., 2015; Judson et al., 2016; Born et al., 2017; Sidorov et al., 2017; Sonzogni et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2019; Copping and Silverman, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Maternal Ube3a deficiency in mice causes increased susceptibility to seizure induction.
source: Many disease relevant phenotypes were reported in these Angelman syndrome models (Margolis et al., 2015; Rotaru et al., 2020; Yang, 2020), and some of them are robust and reproducible in different models and laboratories, including motor impairments (e.g., poor performance in rotarod and open-field tests), decreased innate marble burying and nest building behaviors, cortical hyperexcitability (e.g, poly-spikes in EEG), altered EEG power spectrum and sleep pattern, increased susceptibility to seizure induction, and reduced synaptic long-term potentiation (Jiang et al., 1998; Miura et al., 2002; Weeber et al., 2003; Colas et al., 2005; Yashiro et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2013; Ehlen et al., 2015; Silva-Santos et al., 2015; Judson et al., 2016; Born et al., 2017; Sidorov et al., 2017; Sonzogni et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2019; Copping and Silverman, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Maternal Ube3a deficiency in mice causes reduced synaptic long-term potentiation.
source: Many disease relevant phenotypes were reported in these Angelman syndrome models (Margolis et al., 2015; Rotaru et al., 2020; Yang, 2020), and some of them are robust and reproducible in different models and laboratories, including motor impairments (e.g., poor performance in rotarod and open-field tests), decreased innate marble burying and nest building behaviors, cortical hyperexcitability (e.g, poly-spikes in EEG), altered EEG power spectrum and sleep pattern, increased susceptibility to seizure induction, and reduced synaptic long-term potentiation (Jiang et al., 1998; Miura et al., 2002; Weeber et al., 2003; Colas et al., 2005; Yashiro et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2013; Ehlen et al., 2015; Silva-Santos et al., 2015; Judson et al., 2016; Born et al., 2017; Sidorov et al., 2017; Sonzogni et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2019; Copping and Silverman, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Most neurological functions in Angelman syndrome mouse models require Ube3a during late embryonic and early postnatal development.
source: By genetically reinstating Ube3a expression from the maternal allele at different developmental ages, rescue experiments in mice show that most of these neurological functions require Ube3a during late embryonic and early postnatal development (Silva-Santos et al., 2015; Rotaru et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2019; Sonzogni et al., 2020), suggesting that the therapeutic window for Angelman syndrome may be limited to very young ages.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to rescue experiments.

claim: Reducing Ube3a-ATS levels in mice through genetic manipulations or topoisomerase inhibition results in unsilencing of the paternal Ube3a.
source: Indeed, reducing Ube3a-ATS levels in mice through genetic manipulations or topoisomerase inhibition results in unsilencing of the paternal Ube3a (Huang et al., 2011; Meng et al., 2012; Meng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Antisense oligonucleotides or CRISPR/Cas9 targeting the mouse Ube3a-ATS can upregulate paternal Ube3a expression.
source: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) or CRISPR/Cas9 targeting the mouse Ube3a-ATS can also upregulate paternal Ube3a expression.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is a premise for the current study.

claim: Administering ASO or AAV expressing CRISPR/Cas9 to newborn maternal Ube3a knockout mice rescues a subset of phenotypes.
source: Administering ASO or adeno-associated virus (AAV) expressing CRISPR/Cas9 to newborn, but not older, maternal Ube3a knockout mice rescues a subset of phenotypes (Meng et al., 2015; Wolter et al., 2020; Milazzo et al., 2021; Schmid et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Administering ASO or AAV expressing CRISPR/Cas9 to older maternal Ube3a knockout mice does not rescue phenotypes.
source: Administering ASO or adeno-associated virus (AAV) expressing CRISPR/Cas9 to newborn, but not older, maternal Ube3a knockout mice rescues a subset of phenotypes (Meng et al., 2015; Wolter et al., 2020; Milazzo et al., 2021; Schmid et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Three Phase 1 or Phase 1/2 clinical trials with ASOs targeting UBE3A-ATS are underway.
source: Currently, three Phase 1 or Phase 1/2 clinical trials with ASOs targeting UBE3A-ATS are underway.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and reflects the current state of clinical development.

claim: Expressing an exogenous copy of UBE3A by AAV only rescues a subset of phenotypes when administered postnatally.
source: Another approach is to directly express an exogenous copy of UBE3A by AAV, which also only rescues a subset of phenotypes of maternal Ube3a knockout mice when administered postnatally (Daily et al., 2011; Judson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Angelman syndrome is diagnosed after at least the first 6 months of life and typically between 1 and 4 years of age.
source: This timing of intervention would be difficult because currently Angelman syndrome is diagnosed after at least the first 6 months of life and typically between 1 and 4 years of age (Williams et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Alterations in EEG power spectrum, particularly an increase in the power of low frequency oscillations (1–30 Hz), are well documented in both Angelman syndrome patients and rodent models.
source: Alterations in EEG power spectrum, particularly an increase in the power of low frequency oscillations (i.e., 1–30 Hz), are well documented in both Angelman syndrome patients and rodent models (Born et al., 2017; Sidorov et al., 2017; Frohlich et al., 2019; Born et al., 2021; Copping and Silverman, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The power in the delta range (2–4 Hz) correlates with symptom severity in Angelman syndrome patients.
source: This brain rhythm is a potential biomarker for assessing clinical symptoms because the power in the delta range (2–4 Hz) correlates with symptom severity in Angelman syndrome patients (Hipp et al., 2021; Ostrowski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Sleep disturbance is a prominent feature of Angelman syndrome.
source: Similarly, sleep disturbance, another prominent feature of Angelman syndrome (Spruyt et al., 2018), is also recapitulated in the mouse models (Colas et al., 2005; Ehlen et al., 2015; Copping and Silverman, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Sleep disturbance is recapitulated in Angelman syndrome mouse models.
source: Similarly, sleep disturbance, another prominent feature of Angelman syndrome (Spruyt et al., 2018), is also recapitulated in the mouse models (Colas et al., 2005; Ehlen et al., 2015; Copping and Silverman, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The Ube3atm1Alb allele deletes exon 5 and results in a premature stop codon in exon 6.
source: The widely used mouse model is a Ube3a knockout allele (Ube3atm1Alb, referred to as Ube3aΔe5 here to be distinguished from the new allele) that deletes exon 5 (previously named as exon 2), resulting in a premature stop codon in exon 6 (Jiang et al., 1998; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Exons downstream of the deleted exon 5 in Ube3aΔe5 mice are still transcribed in the brain at levels comparable to wild-type mice.
source: Exons 4, 6, and other exons downstream of the deleted exon 5 were still transcribed in the brains of adult heterozygous maternal (Ube3amΔe5/p+) and homozygous (Ube3amΔe5/pΔe5) mutant mice at a level comparable to wild-type (WT) mice (Figure 1C), possibly due to an escape from nonsense-mediated mRNA decay or an alternative start site.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: The Ube3aΔe6 allele carries a premature stop codon in exon 7.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 was used to delete the largest Ube3a coding exon, exon 6. The resulting allele (Ube3aΔe6) carries a premature stop codon in exon 7 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ube3a mRNA is diminished in the brain of Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice.
source: RT-ddPCR analyses of adult heterozygous maternal mutant mice (Ube3amΔe6/p+) showed that Ube3a mRNA was diminished in the brain and reduced in the liver as compared to WT mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: Ube3a protein levels in different brain regions of Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice were 2–17% of those in WT mice when they were at 6 weeks of age or older.
source: Western blots revealed that Ube3a protein levels in different brain regions of Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice were 2–17% of those in WT mice when they were at 6 weeks of age or older (see below).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and refers to Western blot data presented later.

claim: Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice showed similar rotarod and marble burying phenotypes to previously reported deficits in Ube3amΔe5/p+ mice.
source: Furthermore, Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice showed similar rotarod and marble burying phenotypes to previously reported deficits in Ube3amΔe5/p+ mice (Shi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Ube3a-as ASO decreased Ube3a-ATS transcripts and increased Ube3a mRNA levels in 8-week-old WT mice.
source: Both Ube3a-as ASO and Snord115 ASO decreased Ube3a-ATS transcripts and increased Ube3a mRNA levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Snord115 ASO decreased Ube3a-ATS transcripts and increased Ube3a mRNA levels in 8-week-old WT mice.
source: Both Ube3a-as ASO and Snord115 ASO decreased Ube3a-ATS transcripts and increased Ube3a mRNA levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ube3a-as ASO increased Ube3a-YFP expression in many brain regions of Ube3am+/pYFP mice to 40–90% of that of Ube3amYFP/p+ mice.
source: Ube3a-as ASO and Snord115 ASO increased Ube3a-YFP expression in many brain regions of Ube3am+/pYFP mice to 40–90% and 20–60% of that of Ube3amYFP/p+ mice, respectively (Figure 2A, B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2A, B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Snord115 ASO increased Ube3a-YFP expression in many brain regions of Ube3am+/pYFP mice to 20–60% of that of Ube3amYFP/p+ mice.
source: Ube3a-as ASO and Snord115 ASO increased Ube3a-YFP expression in many brain regions of Ube3am+/pYFP mice to 40–90% and 20–60% of that of Ube3amYFP/p+ mice, respectively (Figure 2A, B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2A, B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both Ube3a-as ASO and Snord115 ASO can broadly reactivate the paternal Ube3a-YFP allele in neurons including GABAergic neurons throughout the mouse brain in vivo.
source: Thus, both Ube3a-as ASO and Snord115 ASO can broadly reactivate the paternal Ube3a-YFP allele in neurons including GABAergic neurons throughout the mouse brain in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the YFP expression data.

claim: At 3 weeks post ASO injection, Ube3a-as ASO increased Ube3a protein levels in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice to about 28–71% of the WT levels in different brain regions.
source: At 3 weeks post ASO injection, Ube3a-as ASO and Snord115 ASO increased Ube3a protein levels in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice to about 28–71% of the WT levels in different brain regions (Figure 3B, D, E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in multiple figures.

claim: At 3 weeks post ASO injection, Snord115 ASO increased Ube3a protein levels in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice to about 28–71% of the WT levels in different brain regions.
source: At 3 weeks post ASO injection, Ube3a-as ASO and Snord115 ASO increased Ube3a protein levels in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice to about 28–71% of the WT levels in different brain regions (Figure 3B, D, E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in multiple figures.

claim: Ube3a-ATS levels were downregulated by 29–73% at 3 weeks post ASO injection in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice.
source: Correlated with this result, Ube3a-ATS levels were downregulated by 29–73% (Figure 4A, B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and Ube3a mRNA levels were increased to about 22–57% of the WT levels (Figure 4A, B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4A, B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ube3a mRNA levels were increased to about 22–57% of the WT levels at 3 weeks post ASO injection in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice.
source: Correlated with this result, Ube3a-ATS levels were downregulated by 29–73% (Figure 4A, B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and Ube3a mRNA levels were increased to about 22–57% of the WT levels (Figure 4A, B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4A, B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effects of Ube3a-as ASO remained stable for at least 10 weeks.
source: The effects of Ube3a-as ASO remained stable for at least 10 weeks.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by longitudinal data in the figures.

claim: The Ube3a protein and Ube3a mRNA levels in Snord115 ASO-treated Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice markedly decreased at 6 weeks post injection.
source: However, the Ube3a protein and Ube3a mRNA levels in Snord115 ASO-treated Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice markedly decreased at 6 weeks post injection and reached to the levels of control ASO-treated Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice in most brain regions by 10 weeks post injection (Figure 3B, D, E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Figure 4A, B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in multiple figures.

claim: Both Ube3a isoforms 2 and 3 were similarly upregulated by Ube3a-as ASO or Snord115 ASO in different brain regions of Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice.
source: Thus, we performed additional Western blot analyses and found that both Ube3a isoforms were similarly upregulated by Ube3a-as ASO or Snord115 ASO in different brain regions of Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 4), confirming the successful reactivation of the critical isoform 3.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Ube3a-ATS levels negatively correlated with Ube3a protein levels in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice.
source: Ube3a-ATS levels negatively correlated with Ube3a protein and Ube3a mRNA levels in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), and Ube3a protein levels positively correlated with Ube3a mRNA levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by correlation analyses in Figure 4C.

claim: Ube3a-ATS levels negatively correlated with Ube3a mRNA levels in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice.
source: Ube3a-ATS levels negatively correlated with Ube3a protein and Ube3a mRNA levels in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), and Ube3a protein levels positively correlated with Ube3a mRNA levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by correlation analyses in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Ube3a protein levels positively correlated with Ube3a mRNA levels in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice.
source: Ube3a-ATS levels negatively correlated with Ube3a protein and Ube3a mRNA levels in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), and Ube3a protein levels positively correlated with Ube3a mRNA levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by correlation analyses in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Control ASO-treated Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice show an increase of power in the 8–25 Hz range compared to control ASO-treated WT mice.
source: Control ASO-treated Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice show an increase of power in the 8–25 Hz range and a decrease of power in the 50–100 Hz range as compared to control ASO-treated WT mice.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 5 and shown in the data.

claim: Control ASO-treated Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice show a decrease of power in the 50–100 Hz range compared to control ASO-treated WT mice.
source: Control ASO-treated Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice show an increase of power in the 8–25 Hz range and a decrease of power in the 50–100 Hz range as compared to control ASO-treated WT mice.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 5 and shown in the data.

claim: Ube3a-as ASO reduces the power in 8–25 Hz and increases the power in 50–100 Hz in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice.
source: Ube3a-as ASO reduces the power in 8–25 Hz and increases the power in 50–100 Hz in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 5 and shown in the data.

claim: Snord115 ASO has a similar effect to Ube3a-as ASO in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice at 3 weeks post ASO injection.
source: Snord115 ASO has a similar effect in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice at 3 weeks post ASO injection.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 5 and shown in the data.

claim: The power ratio (α + β1 + β2)/γ2 was higher in control ASO-treated Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice than control ASO-treated WT mice across all timepoints.
source: We discovered that the power ratio (α + β1 + β2)/γ2 was higher in control ASO-treated Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice than control ASO-treated WT mice across all timepoints (Figure 5E, I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5E and I.

claim: A single ICV injection of Ube3a-ATS-targeted ASOs to Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice upregulates Ube3a proteins including the critical short isoform.
source: Our study reveals that a single ICV injection of Ube3a-ATS-targeted ASOs to Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice, a new rodent model of Angelman syndrome (Shi et al., 2022), upregulates Ube3a proteins including the critical short isoform and restores the EEG power spectrum and sleep pattern for at least 6 weeks, particularly upon treatment at the juvenile age.
